8194.title: Merge Sort
8194.heading: Merge Sort
8194.content:
Merge sort divides an unsorted collection into smaller groups until every group contains one trivially sorted item. It then repeatedly applies a [[Merge Operation]] to combine sorted groups into larger sorted groups.

This [[Divide and Conquer]] structure gives $O(n\log n)$ [[Time Complexity]]. Independent subgroups can be processed on different computers or processors before their results are merged, making the method suitable for large parallel sorts.

8197.title: Merge Operation
8197.heading: Merge Operation
8197.content:
A merge operation combines two already sorted sequences into one sorted sequence. It compares the first remaining item of each sequence, appends the smaller one to the result, and advances within that sequence.

When one input is exhausted, the remaining items of the other can be appended directly. This linear operation is the combining stage of [[Merge Sort]] and is what turns separately solved subproblems into a complete ordered result.

8200.heading: Mercator Scale Variation
8200.content: Mercator scale is true at the Equator in the simple tangent form and increases with the secant of latitude. Areas at high latitude therefore appear much larger than their actual proportions, even though local shape remains conformal. The increasing distortion makes the projection best suited to a limited equatorial or otherwise carefully bounded band.

8206.title: Memristor Computing
8206.heading: Memristor Computing
8206.content:
Memristor computing uses circuit elements whose resistance depends on the history of current that has passed through them. The same physical structure can combine storage with computation, reducing movement between processor and memory.

This organization may ease the [[Processor-Memory Bottleneck]] and support neural-style workloads. Programming it requires thinking in terms of material state and signal dynamics rather than only sequential instructions.

8212.content:

The source identifies [[Process Isolation]], [[Hardware Memory Segmentation]], and [[Virtual Memory Protection]] as complementary mechanisms. Their combined boundary protects application behavior and the confidentiality, integrity, and availability of in-memory data.

8218.title: Memory Preallocation
8218.heading: Memory Preallocation
8218.content:
Memory preallocation reserves request objects and data buffers before they are needed in the latency-sensitive I/O path. Reusing this pool avoids allocator overhead, fragmentation, and unpredictable blocking during bursts.

The pool size must balance wasted capacity against exhaustion. A bounded design also needs explicit behavior when demand temporarily exceeds the reserved resources.

Mechanization joins numerical calculation and logical inference under explicit rules that a machine can execute without human intervention. This ideal motivated formal methods, models of computation, and the development of automatic digital computers.

Mechanization also revealed boundaries. A machine can reproduce a rule-governed process at extraordinary speed, but some questions are undecidable and many practical computations require approximations, judgment, or domain-specific interpretation.

8242.title: Measurement Uncertainty
8242.heading: Measurement Uncertainty
8242.content: Measurement uncertainty states a defensible interval around a reported value rather than claiming unattainable exactness. It may be written as an absolute uncertainty, such as $x\pm\delta x$, or as a fractional or percentage uncertainty. When measurements are combined, their uncertainties must also be propagated so the result reflects the limitations of the original data.

8245.title: Measurement Precision as Cluster Resolution
8245.heading: Measurement Precision as Cluster Resolution
8245.content:
In a longest-common-prefix hierarchy, the number of retained digits sets cluster resolution. Sharing one digit creates broad bins; sharing several creates more selective bins. Reducing recorded precision can thus make values equal at a coarse level and induce a more visibly hierarchical representation.

The book demonstrates this with chemical fingerprints recoded at different precisions. The effect is partly a consequence of encoding, not a discovery independent of the measurement process. A coarse bin can aid search or preprocessing while hiding distinctions needed for scientific interpretation.

8248.title: Measurement Error
8248.heading: Measurement Error
8248.content:
Measurement error is the difference between a sensor reading and the physical quantity it is intended to represent. Systematic error introduces a repeatable bias, while random error produces changing noise or jitter around repeated measurements.

Calibration can reduce modeled systematic error. Filtering can reduce random variation, but often adds computation and delay, so an augmented-reality tracker must balance smoother measurements against temporal registration.

Changing the unit in which a measured quantity is reported does not supply a more accurate observation. Pryor's conversion discussion warns against mistaking displayed numerical resolution for meaningful accuracy; the precision of the original measurement should govern the converted result's reported digits. See [[Conversion Resolution versus Accuracy]].

8254.sourceSearchName: meaningful work under automation meaningful work under automation
8254.title: Meaningful Work Under Automation
8254.heading: Meaningful Work Under Automation
8254.content:
Meaningful work under automation concerns how the removal or transformation of tasks affects purpose, skill, social recognition, autonomy, and participation in a shared activity. Employment supplies income, but its value is not exhausted by wages.

Automation can remove dangerous or monotonous tasks and create more room for care, creativity, or leisure. It can also fragment jobs, reduce judgment, or make people supervise systems they cannot influence. A good outcome depends on how work is redesigned and how society distributes the benefits. [[Human-AI Collaboration]] should therefore be assessed by the quality of the human role, not merely by combined output.

8257.sourceSearchName: meaningful digital consent meaningful digital consent
8257.title: Meaningful Digital Consent
8257.heading: Meaningful Digital Consent
8257.content:
Meaningful digital consent is permission based on a real understanding of what data will be collected, how they will be used, and what consequences may follow. Clicking through a long agreement does not create meaningful choice when access depends on acceptance or future uses cannot be understood.

AI makes consent harder because data can be combined, repurposed, and used to infer traits that were never directly supplied. Consent is therefore only one protection among others. Access rights, purpose limits, explanation, security, and the ability to object to automated decisions remain necessary when an individual cannot realistically negotiate the terms.

Big-data processing also weakens notice when neither the collector nor the person can predict every later correlation. Consent remains relevant, but it cannot carry the entire burden of protecting individual and collective interests.
links: Big Data Law and Individual Rights

8260.title: Meaningful Decision
8260.heading: Meaningful Decision
8260.content:
A meaningful decision is a choice that changes a discernible state, alters future possibilities, matters to a goal, or changes how the player interprets the experience. Its alternatives must differ in mechanical or reflective consequence rather than merely appear different.

Meaningful decisions require some uncertainty and a [[Play Space]] with multiple viable paths. A dominant strategy, equivalent options, or an inevitable outcome turns apparent choice into an illusion and reduces [[Engagement]].

Choices feel integrated when they are made through established [[Game Verb|verbs]] and relationships. A [[Reflective Choice]] may leave the game state unchanged while still making the player consider identity, values, or attitude.

Maxwell's equations relate electric and magnetic fields to charge and current. Their differential form is suited to finite element treatment because it produces field equations over a bounded domain, while their integral form expresses circulation and flux over contours, surfaces, and volumes.

Together with material relations and boundary conditions, they define macroscopic electromagnetic problems. Static, quasi-static, source-free, and time-harmonic cases follow by simplifying their source or time-derivative terms.

Maximum-margin classification chooses a separating hyperplane that maximizes the distance to the nearest training observations from either class. Those closest cases define the attainable margin.

A larger margin provides a geometric form of regularization because many separating boundaries may classify the training data perfectly but differ in robustness. The hard-margin formulation requires separability; overlapping data require penalties for violations.

8290.heading: Maximum Likelihood Estimation
8290.content:
Maximum likelihood estimation selects the parameter value under which the observed data has greatest probability. It converts parameter identification into an optimization problem once a parametric family has been specified.

The result is a point estimate and does not by itself retain uncertainty about nearby values. Unlike a Bayesian estimator, it does not combine the likelihood with an explicit prior over parameters.

The source illustrates the method with Poisson counts: independence turns the joint probability of all observed segment counts into a likelihood for the rate parameter, and the maximizing rate is the sample mean count. The example shows how a distributional assumption determines the optimization target.

8293.sourceSearchName: maximum entropy principle maximum entropy principle
8293.title: Maximum Entropy Principle
8293.heading: Maximum Entropy Principle
8293.content:
The maximum entropy principle selects, among the distributions satisfying stated constraints, the distribution with greatest entropy. It represents the supplied information while avoiding additional distinctions that the constraints do not justify.

The constraints and observable functions remain modeling choices; maximizing entropy does not create knowledge absent from them. The resulting exponential form makes explicit which expectations or macroscopic quantities were imposed.

The prior distinguishes it from maximum likelihood estimation. MAP is useful when a decision requires one assignment, but it can hide uncertainty, multiple modes, and the probability mass surrounding the chosen maximum.

8299.heading: Maximization Step
8299.content:
The maximization step of expectation-maximization chooses parameters that optimize the expected complete-data log likelihood supplied by the expectation step. The updated parameters define the model used in the next iteration.

Alternating this optimization with latent-variable inference couples identification and missing-data estimation. The cycle stops when improvements become sufficiently small or another convergence condition is reached.

8302.title: Maximal Ideal
8302.heading: Maximal Ideal
8302.content:
A maximal ideal is a proper [[Ideal]] that is contained in no other proper ideal. Equivalently, its [[Quotient Ring]] is a [[Field]].

Every proper ideal is contained in at least one maximal ideal. A [[Local Ring]] has exactly one maximal ideal, and its quotient by that ideal is the [[Residue Field]]. Since fields are integral domains, every maximal ideal is a [[Prime Ideal]].

The source relates maximality to field quotients and uses maximal principal ideals in polynomial rings to construct extension fields. Thus maximal ideals become a mechanism for adjoining roots as well as an order-theoretic property.

8308.title: Matrix
8308.heading: Matrix
8308.content:
A matrix is a rectangular arrangement of values organized into horizontal rows and vertical columns. Each position is identified by its row and column, allowing related quantities and transformations to be expressed compactly.

Matrices can represent graph connections, sales data, neural-network parameters, or other structured numerical relationships. [[Matrix Multiplication]] combines compatible matrices, while a [[Vector]] can be treated as the special case of a matrix with one row or one column.

Matrix algebra also includes [[Matrix Addition]], [[Scalar Multiplication of a Matrix]], and [[Matrix Transpose]]. Shape and structure matter: a [[Square Matrix]] may have a [[Determinant]], [[Matrix Inverse]], eigenvalues, and factorizations, while a [[Rectangular Matrix]] naturally represents overdetermined or underdetermined systems.

For statistical modeling, a matrix can place observations in rows and model terms in columns so one equation represents an entire dataset. This representation makes the relationship among a design, its coefficients, fitted values, and residuals explicit.

Finite element formulations use matrix notation to collect element coefficients, nodal unknowns, and loads. Assembly ultimately produces a large simultaneous system in which rows and columns follow the ordering of global degrees of freedom.

8310.title: Matrix Transpose
8310.heading: Document
8310.content:
2026-09-06 19:44

Status: #baby

Tags: [[Matrix and Vector Computation]] · [[Matrix Algebra for Statistical Models]] · [[FEM Mathematical Foundations]]

8311.title: Matrix Transpose
8311.heading: Matrix Transpose
8311.content:
The transpose of a matrix exchanges its rows and columns. If $A$ is an $m\times n$ matrix, then $A^T$ is $n\times m$ and its entries satisfy $(A^T)_{ij}=a_{ji}$.

Transposition reverses the order of a product: $(AB)^T=B^TA^T$. A matrix equal to its transpose is a [[Symmetric Matrix]], while one equal to the negative of its transpose is a [[Skew-Symmetric Matrix]].

The source uses transposition to form dot products, sums of squares, and the normal equations. In R, `t` changes row orientation to column orientation so outcome and design matrices have compatible dimensions for these calculations.

Transposes enter variational finite element expressions when gradient or interpolation vectors form quadratic energy terms and symmetric element matrices. They also reverse the order of products during derivations.

8314.title: Matrix Trace
8314.heading: Matrix Trace
8314.content:
The trace of a square matrix is the sum of its main-diagonal entries: $\operatorname{tr}(A)=\sum_i a_{ii}$.

Trace is unchanged by transposition and similarity transformations, and $\operatorname{tr}(AB)=\operatorname{tr}(BA)$ when both products are defined. Counting multiplicity, it also equals the sum of a matrix's eigenvalues.

8317.heading: Matrix Sketching for Data Streams
8317.content:
Matrix sketching maintains a compact matrix that approximates important properties of a much larger streaming data matrix. The sketch can preserve covariance or projection behavior needed for downstream dimension reduction.

Because its size is bounded independently of stream length, a sketch makes one-pass processing feasible. Approximation guarantees quantify the information sacrificed for memory and speed.

8320.title: Matrix Rank
8320.heading: Matrix Rank
8320.content:
The rank of a matrix is the number of linearly independent rows, which equals the number of linearly independent columns. It can be read as the number of pivots in a [[Row Echelon Form]].

Rank determines how much independent information a matrix contains. A square matrix has an inverse exactly when it has full rank, while rank comparisons of a [[Coefficient Matrix]] and its [[Augmented Matrix]] help determine whether a [[Linear System]] is consistent.

In a design matrix, rank counts the independently estimable columns. If rank is smaller than the number of model terms, the least-squares coefficients are not unique and at least one intended scientific effect cannot be separated from the others.

8323.title: Matrix Norm
8323.heading: Matrix Norm
8323.content:
A matrix norm assigns a nonnegative size to a matrix and is compatible with matrix addition and scalar multiplication. Common induced norms measure the largest column sum, largest row sum, or maximum stretching of Euclidean vector length.

Matrix norms bound products and errors. They are used with the norm of the inverse to define a [[Matrix Condition Number]].

8326.title: Matrix Multiplication
8326.heading: Matrix Multiplication
8326.content:
Matrix multiplication combines two compatible matrices by taking each row from the first matrix with each column from the second. The corresponding values are multiplied and their products summed to form one entry in the result.

The operation expresses many related calculations at once. PageRank uses repeated [[Vector-Matrix Multiplication]], while neural networks can calculate the weighted inputs of many artificial neurons through large matrix operations.

If $A$ has size $m\times n$ and $B$ has size $n\times p$, then $AB$ has size $m\times p$ and entry $(i,j)$ is the dot product of row $i$ of $A$ with column $j$ of $B$. Matrix multiplication is associative and distributive but generally not commutative: even when both products exist, $AB$ need not equal $BA$.

In a linear model, multiplying the design matrix by the coefficient vector produces a fitted value for every experimental unit at once. R uses `%*%` for this operation, distinguishing it from element-wise multiplication.

Finite element equations use matrix products to map nodal unknowns into loads, strains, stresses, gradients, and fluxes. The order of multiplication matters because coefficient, interpolation, and field vectors have specific compatible dimensions.

8328.title: Matrix Inverse

8329.title: Matrix Inverse
8329.heading: Matrix Inverse
8329.content:
An inverse of a square matrix $A$ is a matrix $A^{-1}$ satisfying $AA^{-1}=A^{-1}A=I$. It exists only when $A$ is a [[Nonsingular Matrix]], equivalently when its [[Determinant]] is nonzero.

For a system $Ax=b$, multiplication by the inverse gives $x=A^{-1}b$. In computation, a direct solver or [[LU Decomposition]] is usually preferable to explicitly forming the inverse.

The closed-form least-squares expression includes the inverse of the design cross-product, but the source cautions that explicitly computing it with `solve` can be numerically unstable. A [[QR Decomposition]] is preferred for fitting in practical software.

The primer expresses formal finite element solutions through an inverse of the reduced global matrix. For large assembled systems, solving the equations directly is preferable to explicitly constructing that inverse.

8332.title: Matrix Factorization Recommendation
8332.heading: Matrix Factorization Recommendation
8332.content:
Matrix factorization learns lower-dimensional representations of two kinds of related entities, such as customers and products, from observed interactions. Their learned factors are combined to score pairs that were not directly observed.

In a co-purchase recommender, transaction relationships provide the training signal and candidate items are ranked by predicted score. The score orders recommendations but should not automatically be interpreted as a calibrated probability of purchase.

At large scale, matrix factorization summarizes a sparse user-item matrix with [[Latent Factor Model]] representations. [[Alternating Least Squares]] can fit those factors by switching between user and item updates, a structure that supports parallel execution.

8335.title: Matrix Diagonalization
8335.heading: Matrix Diagonalization
8335.content:
Matrix diagonalization factors a diagonalizable matrix as $A=QDQ^{-1}$, where the columns of $Q$ are eigenvectors and $D$ contains their eigenvalues.

The representation simplifies powers, difference equations, and systems of differential equations because $D^k$ and functions of $D$ act entry by entry. A real symmetric matrix permits [[Orthogonal Diagonalization]].

8338.title: Matrix Determinant
8338.heading: Matrix Determinant
8338.content:
The determinant is a scalar associated with a square [[Matrix]]. It can be expanded along any row or column using signed minors, and a zero determinant identifies a singular matrix.

For a linear system, a nonzero determinant supports a unique solution. In an [[Eigenvalue Problem]], the characteristic equation sets the determinant of the shifted matrix to zero so nontrivial eigenvectors can exist.

8341.sourceSearchName: matrix condition number matrix condition number
8341.title: Matrix Condition Number
8341.heading: Matrix Condition Number
8341.content:
A matrix condition number compares the size of a nonsingular matrix with the size of its inverse, commonly $\kappa(A)=\|A\|\|A^{-1}\|$ for a chosen norm.

A value near one indicates relatively low sensitivity, while a large value warns that small coefficient, right-hand-side, or round-off errors may cause large relative errors in the solution. It measures problem sensitivity rather than algorithm quality.

8342.sourceSearchName: matrix condition number matrix condition number
8342.title: Matrix Condition Number
8342.heading: References

8344.title: Matrix Concatenation
8344.heading: Matrix Concatenation
8344.content:
Matrix concatenation multiplies transformation matrices so several spatial operations can be applied as one composite transform. The resulting matrix preserves the sequence of operations encoded by the multiplication order.

Scale, rotation, and translation therefore cannot be rearranged casually. A world transform that scales, then rotates, then translates describes different behavior from a matrix that performs those operations in another order.

8346.title: Matrix Addition
8346.heading: Document

8347.title: Matrix Addition
8347.heading: Matrix Addition
8347.content:
Matrix addition combines two matrices of the same size by adding corresponding entries. If $A=(a_{ij})$ and $B=(b_{ij})$, then $A+B=(a_{ij}+b_{ij})$. The result has the same dimensions as both inputs.

The operation is commutative and associative, and the [[Zero Matrix]] acts as its additive identity. Matrix subtraction is addition of a [[Scalar Multiplication of a Matrix|scalar multiple]] by $-1$.

During finite element assembly, matrices from elements sharing a degree of freedom contribute by addition to the corresponding global entries. Compatible dimensions and consistent local-to-global numbering are therefore essential.

8350.title: MATLAB Workspace
8350.heading: MATLAB Workspace
8350.content:
The MATLAB workspace is the collection of variables currently stored during a session. Variables can be scalars, vectors, matrices, strings, or other arrays.

Commands create and transform these values, and workspace inspection shows their names, sizes, and current contents. Matrix-oriented variables let the same language express both data and numerical algorithms.

8353.title: MATLAB Vector
8353.heading: MATLAB Vector
8353.content:
A MATLAB vector is a one-dimensional numeric array written as a row or column. Spaces or commas separate row entries, and a semicolon or transpose can create a column.

The [[MATLAB Colon Operator]] efficiently constructs regularly spaced vectors. Vector orientation matters for matrix multiplication even when the same components are present.

8356.title: MATLAB Plot
8356.heading: MATLAB Plot
8356.content:
MATLAB plotting turns vector or matrix data into two- or three-dimensional graphs. A two-dimensional plot pairs vectors of input and output values, while mesh and surface commands use gridded values for functions of two variables.

Labels, axes, markers, multiple curves, and subplots provide context. The numerical sampling chosen through the [[MATLAB Colon Operator]] affects how smoothly a curve or surface is represented.

8358.sourceSearchName: matlab numeric format matlab numeric format
8358.title: MATLAB Numeric Format
8358.heading: Document

8359.sourceSearchName: matlab numeric format matlab numeric format
8359.title: MATLAB Numeric Format
8359.heading: MATLAB Numeric Format
8359.content:
A MATLAB numeric format controls how numbers are displayed, such as short decimal or scientific notation. Changing the format does not change the stored numerical value.

This distinction matters when assessing error: a displayed value may show fewer digits than are retained internally, while actual calculations remain subject to floating-point precision.

8362.heading: MATLAB Function File
8362.content:
A MATLAB function file defines a reusable computation with named inputs and outputs. Local variables support the implementation without requiring repeated manual commands.

Functions package numerical methods such as elimination, interpolation, or iteration behind a consistent call. This separates an algorithm from a particular dataset and makes it easier to test and reuse.

8365.title: MATLAB Matrix
8365.heading: MATLAB Matrix
8365.content:
A MATLAB matrix is entered with spaces or commas between columns and semicolons between rows. Matrix variables are the central data structure of MATLAB.

Standard operators implement linear-algebra operations when dimensions are compatible. [[MATLAB Element-Wise Operator|Element-wise operators]] are distinct and apply the operation separately to corresponding entries.

8368.title: MATLAB Command Window
8368.heading: MATLAB Command Window
8368.content:
The MATLAB Command Window is the interactive interface where expressions and commands are entered and evaluated immediately. It can be used like a calculator or to invoke matrix, plotting, and numerical routines.

Commands create variables in the [[MATLAB Workspace]]. Longer or reusable procedures are better placed in a [[MATLAB Function File]] rather than repeatedly entered interactively.

8371.sourceSearchName: matlab element wise operator matlab element wise operator
8371.title: MATLAB Element-Wise Operator
8371.heading: MATLAB Element-Wise Operator
8371.content:
A MATLAB element-wise operator applies multiplication, division, or exponentiation independently to corresponding array entries. A period distinguishes it from the matrix operator, as in `A.*B`, `A./B`, or `A.^2`.

The arrays must have compatible sizes for the intended component calculation. Confusing `A*B` with `A.*B` can produce a valid but mathematically different result.

8374.title: MATLAB Colon Operator
8374.heading: MATLAB Colon Operator
8374.content:
The MATLAB colon operator creates regularly spaced sequences and selects ranges of array indices. An expression $a:d:b$ starts at $a$, advances by step $d$, and stops without passing $b$.

Used inside parentheses, a colon can select every entry along a dimension. It therefore supports both vector construction and [[MATLAB Array Indexing]].

8377.title: MATLAB Array Indexing
8377.heading: MATLAB Array Indexing
8377.content:
MATLAB array indexing selects or assigns elements by row and column positions. A single colon selects every entry in a dimension, while index vectors select or reorder specified rows or columns.

Assignments can change individual entries, blocks, or entire dimensions. Because MATLAB uses matrix-shaped data, careful index order is essential to preserving the intended structure.

8380.title: Mathematical Pattern
8380.heading: Mathematical Pattern
8380.content:
A mathematical pattern is a regular relationship among values, positions, or operations that can be expressed with a general rule. Searching for a pattern involves comparing cases, identifying what remains constant, and proposing a [[Law of Formation]].

Algebra turns the proposed regularity into a formula that can be tested beyond the examples that suggested it. A list increasing by five may lead to an [[Arithmetic Progression]], while repeated doubling may lead to a [[Geometric Progression]]. Observing several matching cases supports a conjecture, but the rule must also explain why the relationship continues.

8383.title: Mathematical Induction
8383.heading: Mathematical Induction
8383.content:
Mathematical induction proves a statement for every integer from a starting point by establishing a base case and showing that one valid case forces the next. The induction hypothesis is the temporary assumption used in the second step.

The book uses induction for statements about repeated products, polynomial roots, and finite factorizations.

The computation text emphasizes that the base case anchors the implication chain; the inductive implication alone proves none of the individual cases. It applies induction not only to numbers but also to string length, graph size, grammar productions, and the correctness of [[Recursive Algorithm Correctness|recursive algorithms]].

8386.title: Mathematical Generality
8386.heading: Mathematical Generality
8386.content:
The idea that we can take some of the properties of what we're looking at and examining just those specific properties without relying on other properties from the items that our properties came from. 

In algebra, mathematical generality is achieved by replacing particular numbers with a [[Variable]]. The equation (a+b=b+a) captures the commutative behavior illustrated by indefinitely many numerical cases. A symbolic statement can therefore express a reusable relationship without knowing the variables' particular values. This abstraction must still preserve the properties relevant to the problem.

Models are tools rather than complete answers: they cannot decide the desired experience or eliminate all interaction effects in a complex game. Their predictions still need designer judgment and [[Playtesting]].

8404.heading: Massive-Domain Stream Classification
8404.content:
Massive-domain stream classification handles categorical attributes whose possible values are too numerous to maintain a separate statistic for every value-class combination. New values may also appear continually.

Compact summaries, hashing, sketches, or selective counting replace complete frequency tables. The representation must preserve enough class association to predict while keeping memory independent of the expanding domain size.

8407.heading: Mass-Spring Oscillator
8407.content: An ideal mass-spring oscillator obeys [[Hooke's Law]], so displacement from equilibrium produces the restoring force $F=-kx$. Its angular frequency is $\omega=\sqrt{k/m}$ and its period is $T=2\pi\sqrt{m/k}$. Increasing stiffness shortens the period, while increasing the oscillating mass lengthens it.

8410.heading: Markov Random Field Classification
8410.content:
Markov random field classification uses an undirected graph to encode local conditional independencies. The joint distribution factorizes over cliques through compatibility potentials rather than directed conditional probabilities.

This formulation is useful when relationships are symmetric or no causal ordering is appropriate. Classification requires estimating or approximating the distribution of labels given observations, and cycles can make exact normalization and inference difficult.

8413.title: Markov Localization
8413.heading: Markov Localization
8413.content:
Markov localization estimates a robot's position from a sequence of actions and observations. A motion model predicts where the robot may have moved, while a sensor model corrects that belief using perceived features.

Representing location as a probability distribution permits multiple competing positions to remain possible. Repeated Bayesian updates concentrate or redistribute that belief as new evidence arrives.

8416.heading: Markov Decision Process
8416.content:
A Markov decision process combines probabilistic state transitions with actions and rewards. A policy specifies how actions are selected so that expected cumulative reward is optimized over time.

The Markov assumption makes the next state depend on the current state and action rather than the entire history. When the current state is not directly known, decisions must instead operate on a belief distribution.

8419.title: Markov Cluster Algorithm
8419.heading: Markov Cluster Algorithm
8419.content:
The Markov Cluster Algorithm simulates flow on a graph by alternating expansion and inflation of a stochastic matrix. Expansion spreads transition probability along longer paths, while inflation strengthens high-probability flows and suppresses weak ones.

Repeated operations separate regions in which random walks circulate readily. The inflation parameter controls granularity: stronger inflation tends to produce more and smaller communities.

8422.title: Marker Tracking
8422.heading: Marker Tracking
8422.content:
Marker tracking estimates camera or object pose from a deliberately designed visual target. A square marker provides a high-contrast boundary for detection, an interior pattern for identity and orientation, and four known planar corners for geometric estimation.

After detection, the system estimates a homography and derives pose using the calibrated camera model. Markers simplify correspondence but require the physical environment to be prepared and the target to remain visible.

8425.title: Marginalization Rule
8425.heading: Marginalization Rule
8425.content:
The marginalization rule removes a variable by summing its joint probabilities across every possible value, or by integrating when the variable is continuous. For discrete $Y$, $P(X)=\sum_y P(X,Y=y)$.

In a Bayesian question, free variables are not assumed irrelevant; their possible values are accumulated. The computational difficulty often comes from the size of this summed or integrated space.

8428.heading: Marker Set Validation
8428.content:
Marker set validation checks whether the returns produced by a [[Linguistic Marker Set]] actually represent the intended concept. Researchers inspect usage, associations, variation, and false positives instead of assuming that a keyword match is meaningful.

Validation is especially important when definitions and proximity windows change results sharply. Explicit assumptions help reviewers judge conclusions even when the full corpus or analytical implementation is difficult to reproduce.

8431.title: Marker Detection
8431.heading: Marker Detection
8431.content:
Marker detection locates candidate fiducial targets in a camera image. For a black square marker on a light background, thresholding separates dark pixels, connected contours identify regions, and geometric tests retain quadrilateral shapes with plausible corners.

The interior pattern is then sampled to identify the marker and determine its orientation. The resulting ordered corner correspondences supply the image measurements used for pose estimation.

8434.title: Marginal Probability
8434.heading: Marginal Probability
8434.content:
A marginal probability is the distribution of selected variables after the other variables in a joint distribution have been summed or integrated out. It answers a question that does not condition on or retain those omitted variables.

For discrete variables, the probabilities of every compatible value of the removed variables are added. The result remains normalized over the variables that stay in the question.

8437.title: Marginal Maximum A Posteriori
8437.heading: Marginal Maximum A Posteriori
8437.content:
Marginal maximum a posteriori inference first sums or integrates designated free variables and then maximizes the resulting marginal posterior over searched variables. It differs from maximizing all variables jointly and discarding some afterward.

The distinction matters because marginalization rewards an assignment supported by a large region of alternatives, whereas joint maximization may favor one sharp configuration with little surrounding probability mass.

8440.heading: Margin Maximizing Discriminant Analysis
8440.content:
Margin maximizing discriminant analysis learns several orthogonal projection directions that separate labeled classes with large margins. It extends the support-vector objective from one separating direction to a multidimensional embedding.

Slack variables permit overlap, while an orthogonality constraint prevents the learned directions from collapsing onto the same axis. Euclidean distance after projection becomes the task-specific metric used for comparison.

8443.heading: MapReduce-Based Mining
8443.content:
MapReduce-based mining divides data or candidate evaluation among mapper tasks and combines local results in reducers. The model provides cluster distribution and failure recovery for scans over large collections.

Repeated mining passes can incur substantial job startup, shuffle, and disk costs, so algorithm design should reduce iterations and the amount of intermediate data.

8446.title: MapReduce
8446.heading: MapReduce
8446.content:
MapReduce is a distributed computation pattern that maps input partitions into intermediate records and reduces grouped records into results. Systems such as Pig and Hive can generate sequences of these jobs from higher-level transformations.

The model automates parallel work and data redistribution, but separate jobs impose overhead and typically reread intermediate state. Algorithms with repeated rounds therefore benefit from caching and long-running workers.
